title: Symplectic Forms

We now turn to the opposite extreme from inner products: forms for which every vector is orthogonal to itself.

:::definition{9.7.1} Symplectic form
A ***symplectic form*** on a vector space $V$ over a field $k$ is a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form $B$ on $V$. When $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, alternating forms are the same as skew-symmetric ones, so a symplectic form is just a nondegenerate skew-symmetric bilinear form.
:::

:::example{9.7.2} The standard symplectic form
The form $b((x_1, x_2), (y_1, y_2)) = x_1 y_2 - x_2 y_1$ on $k^2$ (Example [9.1.4](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#example-9-1-4)) is symplectic. More generally, on $k^{2n}$ with coordinates $(x_1, y_1, \ldots, x_n, y_n)$, the ***standard symplectic form*** is $$B\big((x, y), (x', y')\big) = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i y_i' - y_i x_i').$$ Its matrix is block diagonal, $$\Omega_{2n} = \begin{pmatrix} \Omega_2 & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & \Omega_2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Omega_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$ It is alternating (the terms of $B(v, v)$ cancel in pairs) and nondegenerate ($\det \Omega_{2n} = 1$).
:::

:::note
When $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, there is a quick reason why symplectic forms exist only in even dimension: the matrix $A$ of a skew-symmetric form on a space of dimension $m$ satisfies $\det A = \det A^t = \det(-A) = (-1)^m \det A$, so if $m$ is odd then $2\det A = 0$ and $\det A = 0$. The next theorem proves much more, in every characteristic.
:::

:::theorem{9.7.3} Symplectic bases
Let $B$ be a symplectic form on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over any field $k$. Then $\dim V = 2n$ is even, and $V$ has a basis $(e_1, f_1, \ldots, e_n, f_n)$ such that $$B(e_i, e_j) = B(f_i, f_j) = 0, \qquad B(e_i, f_j) = \delta_{ij} = -B(f_j, e_i)$$ for all $i, j$. In such a ***symplectic basis***, the matrix of $B$ is $\Omega_{2n}$.
:::

:::proof
Induction on $\dim V$. If $V = 0$, take $n = 0$ and the empty basis. Otherwise pick any nonzero $e_1 \in V$. Since $B$ is nondegenerate, the functional $B(e_1, \cdot)$ is nonzero, so there is $f \in V$ with $B(e_1, f) \neq 0$; set $f_1 = f / B(e_1, f)$, so that $B(e_1, f_1) = 1$, and $B(f_1, e_1) = -1$ because alternating forms are skew-symmetric. The vectors $e_1, f_1$ are linearly independent: if $f_1 = c e_1$, then $B(e_1, f_1) = c B(e_1, e_1) = 0$.

Let $U = \operatorname{span}(e_1, f_1)$. Then $U \cap U^\perp = \{0\}$: if $v = a e_1 + b f_1$ satisfies $B(v, e_1) = B(v, f_1) = 0$, then $0 = B(v, e_1) = -b$ and $0 = B(v, f_1) = a$. Since $B$ is nondegenerate, $\dim U^\perp = \dim V - 2$ (Lemma [9.1.30](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#lemma-9-1-30)), so $$V = U \oplus U^\perp.$$

The restriction of $B$ to $U^\perp$ is alternating, and it is nondegenerate: if $w \in U^\perp$ satisfies $B(w, w') = 0$ for all $w' \in U^\perp$, then, since also $B(w, u) = 0$ for all $u \in U$, $B(w, \cdot)$ vanishes on $U + U^\perp = V$, so $w = 0$. By induction, $\dim U^\perp = 2(n - 1)$ is even, and $U^\perp$ has a basis $(e_2, f_2, \ldots, e_n, f_n)$ with the required relations among themselves. The remaining relations $B(e_1, x) = B(f_1, x) = 0$ for $x \in \{e_j, f_j\}$, $j \geq 2$, hold because $x \in U^\perp$ and $B$ is skew-symmetric. So $(e_1, f_1, \ldots, e_n, f_n)$ is a symplectic basis, and $\dim V = 2n$.
:::

:::corollary{9.7.4} Uniqueness of symplectic forms
Any two symplectic forms on vector spaces of the same finite dimension are equivalent. In matrix terms, if $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$, every invertible skew-symmetric matrix $A \in \mcM_{2n \times 2n}(k)$ satisfies $P^t A P = \Omega_{2n}$ for some invertible $P$.
:::

:::proof
Map a symplectic basis of one space to a symplectic basis of the other. For the matrix statement, apply the theorem to $B(x, y) = x^t A y$ on $k^{2n}$ and use Proposition [9.1.6](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-6), with $P$ the matrix whose columns are the symplectic basis.
:::

:::note
Compare with symmetric forms: over $\RR$ they are classified by the signature, and over $\QQ$ the classification involves number theory. Nondegenerate alternating forms, by contrast, have a single normal form over every field, determined by the dimension alone.
:::

:::definition{9.7.5} Symplectic group
Let $B$ be a symplectic form on $V$ with $\dim V = 2n$. The ***symplectic group*** of $(V, B)$ is $$\mathrm{Sp}(V, B) = \{T \in \GL(V) : B(T(u), T(v)) = B(u, v) \text{ for all } u, v \in V\}.$$ The ***symplectic group*** $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, k)$ is $\{A \in \GL_{2n}(k) : A^t \Omega_{2n} A = \Omega_{2n}\}$.
:::

:::proposition{9.7.6} The symplectic group
$\mathrm{Sp}(V, B)$ is a subgroup of $\GL(V)$, and any linear $T : V \to V$ with $B(T(u), T(v)) = B(u, v)$ for all $u, v$ is automatically invertible. Choosing a symplectic basis identifies $\mathrm{Sp}(V, B)$ with $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, k)$.
:::

:::proof
If $T(u) = 0$, then $B(u, v) = B(T(u), T(v)) = 0$ for all $v$, so $u = 0$; thus $T$ is injective, hence invertible. The identity preserves $B$; composites of maps preserving $B$ preserve $B$; and $B(T^{-1}(u), T^{-1}(v)) = B(T(T^{-1}(u)), T(T^{-1}(v))) = B(u, v)$. Finally, if $M$ is the matrix of $T$ in a symplectic basis and $x, y$ are coordinate vectors, then $B(T(u), T(v)) = (Mx)^t \Omega_{2n} (My) = x^t M^t \Omega_{2n} M y$, and this equals $x^t \Omega_{2n} y$ for all $x, y$ iff $M^t \Omega_{2n} M = \Omega_{2n}$. So $T \mapsto M$, which is an isomorphism $\GL(V) \cong \GL_{2n}(k)$, carries $\mathrm{Sp}(V, B)$ onto $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, k)$.
:::

:::example{9.7.7} $\mathrm{Sp}(2, k) = \mathrm{SL}_2(k)$
For $A = \begin{psmallmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{psmallmatrix}$, a direct computation gives $$A^t \Omega_2 A = \begin{pmatrix} a & c \\ b & d \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c & d \\ -a & -b \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & ad - bc \\ -(ad - bc) & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \det(A)\, \Omega_2.$$ So $A \in \mathrm{Sp}(2, k)$ iff $\det A = 1$. Geometrically, over $\RR$, a linear map of the plane preserves the signed-area form iff it preserves signed area. In every dimension, taking determinants in $A^t \Omega_{2n} A = \Omega_{2n}$ gives $\det(A)^2 = 1$ for $A \in \mathrm{Sp}(2n, k)$.
:::

## <span class="num">9.7.1</span> Hermitian Forms as Real Forms

A complex vector space can be regarded as a real vector space of twice the dimension. Under this change of viewpoint, a Hermitian form splits into a symmetric form and an alternating form, and the unitary group appears as an intersection of real groups.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, and let $V_{\RR}$ denote $V$ regarded as a real vector space. If $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ is a basis of $V$ over $\CC$, then $\{e_1, ie_1, \ldots, e_n, ie_n\}$ is a basis of $V_{\RR}$ over $\RR$ (since $\sum (a_j + i b_j) e_j = \sum (a_j e_j + b_j\, ie_j)$ for real $a_j, b_j$), so $\dim_{\RR} V_{\RR} = 2n$. Let $J : V_{\RR} \to V_{\RR}$ be multiplication by $i$; it is $\RR$-linear with $J^2 = -\id$. An $\RR$-linear map $T : V_{\RR} \to V_{\RR}$ is $\CC$-linear iff $T \circ J = J \circ T$, since $(a + ib)v = av + bJ(v)$.

:::proposition{9.7.8} Decomposition of Hermitian forms
Let $H$ be a Hermitian form on $V$. Define $G, B : V_{\RR} \times V_{\RR} \to \RR$ by $$G(u, v) = \operatorname{Re} H(u, v), \qquad B(u, v) = \operatorname{Im} H(u, v),$$ so that $H = G + iB$. Then:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $G$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $V_{\RR}$.
2. $B$ is an alternating bilinear form on $V_{\RR}$.
3. $G(Ju, Jv) = G(u, v)$, $B(Ju, Jv) = B(u, v)$, $B(u, v) = G(Ju, v)$, and $G(u, v) = B(u, Jv)$ for all $u, v$.
4. $H$ is nondegenerate iff $G$ is nondegenerate iff $B$ is nondegenerate.
5. If $H$ is a Hermitian inner product, then $G$ is an inner product on $V_{\RR}$ and $B$ is a symplectic form on $V_{\RR}$.
:::

:::proof
(i) $H$ is additive in each variable, and $H(au, v) = aH(u, v) = H(u, av)$ for real $a$; since $\operatorname{Re}$ is $\RR$-linear, $G$ is $\RR$-bilinear. Symmetry: $G(v, u) = \operatorname{Re} \ol{H(u, v)} = \operatorname{Re} H(u, v) = G(u, v)$.

(ii) Similarly $B$ is $\RR$-bilinear, and $B(v, v) = \operatorname{Im} H(v, v) = 0$ since $H(v, v)$ is real.

(iii) $H(iu, iv) = \ol{i}\, i\, H(u, v) = H(u, v)$, which gives the first two identities. Next, $H(iu, v) = -i H(u, v)$, so $G(Ju, v) = \operatorname{Re}(-iH(u, v)) = \operatorname{Im} H(u, v) = B(u, v)$. Finally $H(u, iv) = iH(u, v)$, so $B(u, Jv) = \operatorname{Im}(iH(u, v)) = \operatorname{Re} H(u, v) = G(u, v)$.

(iv) Replacing $v$ by $Jv$ in $G(u, v) = B(u, Jv)$ gives $G(u, Jv) = B(u, J^2 v) = -B(u, v)$. Suppose $H$ is nondegenerate. If $G(u, \cdot) = 0$, then $B(u, v) = -G(u, Jv) = 0$ for all $v$, so $H(u, \cdot) = 0$ and $u = 0$. If $B(u, \cdot) = 0$, then $G(u, v) = B(u, Jv) = 0$ for all $v$, so again $H(u, \cdot) = 0$ and $u = 0$. Conversely, if $G$ is nondegenerate and $H(u, \cdot) = 0$, then $G(u, \cdot) = \operatorname{Re} H(u, \cdot) = 0$, so $u = 0$; the same argument works for $B$.

(v) $G(v, v) = H(v, v) > 0$ for $v \neq 0$, so $G$ is an inner product, and $B$ is alternating by (ii) and nondegenerate by (iv).
:::

:::proposition{9.7.9} Two out of three
Let $H$ be a nondegenerate Hermitian form on $V$, with $G$ and $B$ as above, and let $T : V_{\RR} \to V_{\RR}$ be $\RR$-linear. Consider the conditions:

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $T$ preserves $G$: $G(T(u), T(v)) = G(u, v)$ for all $u, v$;
2. $T$ preserves $B$;
3. $T$ is $\CC$-linear: $TJ = JT$.

Any two of them imply the third. Moreover, $T$ preserves $H$ iff (a) and (b) hold.
:::

:::proof
(a) and (c) imply (b): $B(T(u), T(v)) = G(JT(u), T(v)) = G(TJ(u), T(v)) = G(Ju, v) = B(u, v)$.

(b) and (c) imply (a): $G(T(u), T(v)) = B(T(u), JT(v)) = B(T(u), TJ(v)) = B(u, Jv) = G(u, v)$.

(a) and (b) imply (c): first, $T$ is injective (if $T(u) = 0$, then $G(u, v) = G(T(u), T(v)) = 0$ for all $v$, so $u = 0$ since $G$ is nondegenerate), hence surjective. For all $u, v$, $$G(JT(u), T(v)) = B(T(u), T(v)) = B(u, v) = G(Ju, v) = G(TJ(u), T(v)).$$ So $G(JT(u) - TJ(u), x) = 0$ for every $x = T(v) \in V_{\RR}$, and $JT(u) = TJ(u)$ by nondegeneracy of $G$.

The last statement holds because $H = G + iB$ with $G$ and $B$ real-valued.
:::

:::corollary{9.7.10} The unitary group as an intersection
Identify $\CC^n$ with $\RR^{2n}$ by $(z_1, \ldots, z_n) \mapsto (x_1, y_1, \ldots, x_n, y_n)$, where $z_j = x_j + iy_j$. For the standard Hermitian inner product $H(z, w) = \sum \ol{z_j} w_j$, the form $G$ is the standard inner product of $\RR^{2n}$ and $B$ is the standard symplectic form of Example [9.7.2](/notes/math-55a/9-7-symplectic-forms#example-9-7-2). Regarding $\GL_n(\CC)$ as the subgroup of $\GL_{2n}(\RR)$ of matrices commuting with $J$, $$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{U}(n) &= \mathrm{O}(2n) \cap \mathrm{Sp}(2n, \RR) \cap \GL_n(\CC) \\
&= \mathrm{O}(2n) \cap \GL_n(\CC) = \mathrm{Sp}(2n, \RR) \cap \GL_n(\CC) = \mathrm{O}(2n) \cap \mathrm{Sp}(2n, \RR).
\end{aligned}$$
:::

:::proof
With $z_j = x_j + iy_j$ and $w_j = x_j' + iy_j'$, $$\ol{z_j}\, w_j = (x_j - iy_j)(x_j' + iy_j') = (x_j x_j' + y_j y_j') + i(x_j y_j' - y_j x_j'),$$ so $G$ is the dot product on $\RR^{2n}$ and $B$ is the standard symplectic form. Thus $\mathrm{O}(2n)$ and $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, \RR)$ are the groups of real-linear maps preserving $G$ and $B$, respectively. The group $\mathrm{U}(n)$ consists of the $\CC$-linear maps preserving $H$, i.e., those satisfying (a), (b), and (c) of Proposition [9.7.9](/notes/math-55a/9-7-symplectic-forms#proposition-9-7-9), and by that proposition any two of the three conditions suffice.
:::

:::exercise{9.7.11} Bilinear and symplectic forms
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Find the signature of the quadratic form $Q(x, y, z) = xy + yz + zx$ on $\RR^3$, by constructing an orthogonal basis as in Theorem [9.6.6](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#theorem-9-6-6).
2. Let $B$ be a symplectic form on a vector space $V$ of dimension $2n$. A subspace $L \subseteq V$ is ***isotropic*** if $B(u, v) = 0$ for all $u, v \in L$, i.e., $L \subseteq L^\perp$. Show that every isotropic subspace has dimension at most $n$, and that isotropic subspaces of dimension $n$ exist.

:::solution
**(1)** The symmetric bilinear form is $$B(u, w) = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(u_1 w_2 + u_2 w_1 + u_2 w_3 + u_3 w_2 + u_3 w_1 + u_1 w_3\big).$$ Take $e_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, with $Q(e_1) = 1 \neq 0$. Then $B(e_1, w) = \frac{1}{2}(w_1 + w_2 + 2w_3)$, so $e_1^\perp = \{w : w_1 + w_2 + 2w_3 = 0\}$. In this plane take $e_2 = (1, -1, 0)$, with $Q(e_2) = -1$, and $e_3 = (1, 1, -1)$, with $Q(e_3) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1$. They are orthogonal: $$B(e_2, e_3) = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(1 - 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 - 1\big) = 0.$$ So in the orthogonal basis $\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}$ the matrix of $B$ is $\diag(1, -1, -1)$, and the signature is $(1, 2)$. (Equivalently, the matrix $\frac{1}{2}\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1, -\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}$.)

**(2)** By Lemma [9.1.30](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#lemma-9-1-30), $\dim L^\perp = 2n - \dim L$. If $L \subseteq L^\perp$, then $\dim L \leq 2n - \dim L$, so $\dim L \leq n$. In a symplectic basis $(e_1, f_1, \ldots, e_n, f_n)$, the subspace $\operatorname{span}(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ is isotropic, since $B(e_i, e_j) = 0$ for all $i, j$, and has dimension $n$.
:::
:::
